# MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents

Jingwei Song  Zhisheng Chen  Bingfan Zeng  Jing Tang  Yubo Hou
 Jinhao Jing  Zhengwei Xie  Linfeng Zhang Shanghai Jiao Tong University
 University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences  South China University
of Technology  Huazhong University of Science and Technology  Beihang
University  The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen)  University
of Science and Technology of China u3638265@connect.hku.hk,
zhisheng.researcher@gmail.com

###### Abstract

A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling
agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist
beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or
successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable
capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from
carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution
failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark
with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12
primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains,
together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer.
The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines
stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target
roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent
artifact to cross the source–target boundary. For each probe, no-prior,
related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under
matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and
VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent
direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants,
while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve
either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and
all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early
wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities
unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable,
transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at
[https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source](https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source).

## 1 Introduction

One of the central ambitions of autonomous intelligence is recursive
self-improvement (RSI) ([Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)): an agent should
use experience from its own actions to become more capable over time.
The goal is larger than learning one policy or storing one successful
trajectory. An RSI system should turn experience into a capability,
retain it, and apply it when the task, world, or required action
changes. This loop is central to long-horizon autonomy: as tasks become
harder, the agent must build on what it has already learned.

This view differs from evaluation settings in which training is
separated from testing and improvement is summarized by a single score
([Ren et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)). For RSI, the important question is
whether a gain remains useful after the original interaction has ended.
A capability should survive a change in local conditions, help with a
related goal, and combine with actions that were not part of the source
task. RSI is therefore a systems problem: learning, memory, planning,
and physical interaction must work together, while the resulting gain
remains visible and attributable.

Embodied agents make this problem concrete and difficult. Their behavior
depends on both internal state and physical state. A later success may
reflect a tool left in the inventory, a changed world, a favorable
location, or more source interaction rather than a reusable capability.
A useful benchmark must therefore show that improvement survives a reset
and appears in observable behavior.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We study this question through later behavior. A memory, skill file, or
model update shows that an agent changed internally. It does not show
that the agent gained a useful capability ([Li et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib25); [Park et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib27)). The evidence must link internal change to later
action. It must also distinguish capability from favorable execution. To
test that claim, we compare target behavior after a world reset and
check both task outcomes and stage-level records.

Existing benchmarks address parts of this problem. MCU ([Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib3)) evaluates diverse and combined Minecraft tasks with
automatic verification. LifelongAgentBench ([Zheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)), EvoAgentBench ([Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)), and
PAST-Bench ([Xue et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)) study learning across tasks,
transfer, and persistent state in other settings. Embodied evaluation
also needs to separate world resources from agent state, match source
budgets, and record where a task chain fails ([Ni et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Cheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib21); [Luo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib22)). Otherwise, a score difference may reflect an easier
world, more source interaction, or an early failure that hides later
behavior.

Minecraft makes these controls practical. Collecting resources, crafting
tools, and using them create visible task dependencies. A task-state
graph represents these relations, and environment evidence verifies each
stage. Resetting the world and inventory removes physical carryover,
while stage records show progress before a chain stops ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23); [Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)).

We introduce MC-EvoBench to evaluate embodied RSI in Minecraft.
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
shows its mechanism: measure progress, transfer only a declared agent
artifact, and use matched controls to assess experience gains.
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
compares this design with representative Minecraft benchmarks ([Guss et
al., 2019](#bib.bib7); [Fan et al., 2022](#bib.bib8); [Hill et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). MC-EvoBench provides
a task catalog, verifiers, and three short probe families for
wood-species crafting, wooden-tool transfer, and stone-tool transfer.
The framework can study capability formation, transfer, retention, and
composition. This paper focuses on forward transfer between
graph-related tasks.

Table 1: Minecraft benchmark comparison for embodied RSI.

Our main contributions are as follows:

1.  1.  Embodied RSI as attributable capability change. We formalize an
        agent as a policy, a persistent state, and an update rule, and
        separate this persistent state from the world state. A gain counts
        as experience-driven only when it appears after the target world is
        reset, only a declared artifact crosses the source–target boundary,
        and matched unrelated and shuffled sources rule out alternative
        explanations.
2.  2.  MC-EvoBench, an executable audit of experience-driven improvement.
        It instantiates this definition in Minecraft with a task-state graph
        of 80 tasks, 111 states, and 369 typed edges organized into 19
        chains; stage-level verifiers with three complementary metrics, Task
        Success Rate (TSR), Weighted Graph Progress (WGP), and Verified
        Milestone Progress (VMP); and a four-condition paired protocol with
        matched environment-step budgets and provenance records.
3.  3.  Controlled evidence on embodied transfer. Controller-based agents
        clearly outperform planner-backed variants in direct capability.
        Under matched controls, the reference method shows no stable
        transfer gain, even though its related sources earn more verified
        progress and, on the longer probes, more computation, and early
        wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks leave later capabilities
        unobserved. Future RSI methods must therefore first clear these
        execution bottlenecks, and their gains should be claimed only after
        a controlled audit.

## 2 Related Work

##### Minecraft and embodied-agent benchmarks.

Minecraft combines visual control, persistent resources, and tasks with
many prerequisites. MineDojo provides a large open-world task collection
and a knowledge base that supports broad embodied-agent research ([Fan
et al., 2022](#bib.bib8)). BEDD extends MineRL ([Guss et al.,
2019](#bib.bib7)) with demonstrations and evaluation for tasks whose
success can be difficult to describe with a single exact goal.
MinePlanner focuses on long-horizon planning in large Minecraft worlds,
while OpenHA studies open-source hierarchical agents and their execution
in the same environment ([Hill et al., 2023](#bib.bib9); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)). Voyager uses a curriculum, a skill library, and
environment feedback for continued exploration and skill reuse,
including in a new world ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)). MCU
evaluates a broad set of tasks, their combinations, and automatic
assessment ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib3)). Together, these benchmarks
cover open-world interaction, planning, task diversity, and automatic
verification. They do not, however, isolate whether a controlled source
interaction causes a later improvement after the target world is reset.

##### Lifelong learning and self-evolving agents.

Several recent benchmarks study improvement across tasks and the use of
stored experience. LifelongAgentBench tests skill gain, retention, and
transfer across databases, operating systems, and knowledge graphs
([Zheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)). EvoAgentBench uses agent traces to
identify abilities and groups tasks by shared procedures, making
transfer between related tasks explicit ([Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)).
PAST-Bench compares runs with and without persistent state and tracks
how experience is saved and reused in personal-agent settings ([Xue et
al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). These studies establish useful ideas for
measuring persistence and transfer, but their tasks do not expose the
same physical-state confounds as embodied environments. In Minecraft, an
apparent gain can instead come from a carried tool, a modified world, or
a different starting location. MC-EvoBench addresses this boundary by
resetting inventory and world changes while allowing only a declared
agent artifact to transfer. Its task-state graph makes prerequisites and
progress visible.

##### Memory-mediated improvement and benchmark position.

Memory systems provide a practical mechanism for experience-driven
improvement. Reflexion ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib12)) stores
language feedback from failed attempts and uses it to guide later
decisions. Agent Workflow Memory extracts reusable procedures from
interaction traces for later tasks ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)).
Skill libraries and model updates offer related ways to preserve
information beyond a single episode. These methods show how an agent can
store and retrieve experience, but reuse alone does not establish that a
capability transferred. MC-EvoBench treats experience-driven improvement
as an attribution problem. It separates source and target episodes,
resets the physical state, and transfers only a declared artifact.
Matched source conditions, verifier predicates, and stage records
distinguish capability transfer from carried-over resources and partial
execution.

## 3 MC-EvoBench Framework and Benchmark Design

MC-EvoBench tests whether experience changes later behavior. To support
that claim, it resets the target world, checks outcomes against
environment evidence, and compares matched source conditions.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Target and State Boundary ‣ 3 MC-EvoBench Framework and Benchmark Design ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
shows how these parts work together. Panel (a) follows the agent from
source interaction to target evaluation. Panel (b) shows the tasks,
states, relations, chains, and environment profiles that define each
test.

### 3.1 Evaluation Target and State Boundary

![Refer to caption](2610.13829v1/overview.png)

Figure 2: Benchmark design of MC-EvoBench. Panel (a) follows a paired
evaluation from source interaction and artifact formation to
target-world reset, target execution, stage verification, and metric
reporting. Panel (b) shows how the task catalog is organized into tasks,
states, relations, chains, and profiles. These components support
graph-based progress measurement, controlled transfer probes, and
coverage of embodied capabilities across long-horizon task chains.

We ask whether controlled source interaction improves performance on a
later target task in a reset world. A stored memory or model update
cannot answer this question by itself. We represent an agent as
$`A=(\pi,z,U)`$: $`\pi`$ selects actions from observations and goals,
$`z`$ is the state the method can retain, and $`U`$ updates that state
from experience. Source experience $`E_{S}`$ produces
$`z_{S}=U(z_{0},E_{S})`$. The evaluator records and freezes $`z_{S}`$
before the target run. No source resources, positions, world edits,
route information, or success markers enter the target.

World state includes inventory, tools, resources, position, terrain, and
world changes. Persistent agent state may include memories, prompts,
replay data, checkpoints, or model updates. Every target run starts with
the same registered world and inventory settings. Thus, source tools and
world changes cannot explain a target score difference. A stored
artifact provides evidence of a gain only when the target verifier also
records a change in behavior.

### 3.2 Task-State Graph

MC-EvoBench represents task dependencies and observable resource flow
with

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       G=(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{E}),
       ```                                       |     |

Here, $`\mathcal{T}`$ contains tasks, $`\mathcal{S}`$ contains
observable states, and $`\mathcal{E}`$ contains typed relations. States
include items, tools, locations, structures, and task completion. The
graph describes what tasks require, produce, or consume without
prescribing an action sequence. These three relation types form the
strict execution graph. The remaining types, enables and abstracts_to,
describe possible capability links and task categories; neither proves
transfer.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Task–state graph ‣ Appendix B Task Construction and Composition ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
defines each edge type and gives their counts.

Tasks form stage chains $`C=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K})`$. Each stage has
a goal that the verifier checks against run evidence. The chain shows
prerequisites and where execution stops; the agent remains free to
choose its actions. Stage records reveal partial progress even when the
final goal is not reached. Catalog and probe chains use the same task
definitions and verifier rules. Reset settings, retained state, and step
budgets are fixed before evaluation.

### 3.3 Paired Protocol and Metrics

Each comparison has a source phase and a target phase. The source agent
interacts with registered tasks and forms $`z_{S}`$. The evaluator then
resets the target world and inventory, freezes $`z_{S}`$, and runs the
target task with the same verifier. Four target conditions serve
different purposes. No-prior provides a baseline; related experience
tests for a change; unrelated experience tests whether that change
depends on task relevance; and shuffled related experience tests whether
task order matters. We record source steps, termination, artifact
identity, and target outcomes. Source episodes restart after early
termination until the declared budget is used.

The verifier records the evidence for each stage, changes in resources,
pass status, and why the run stopped. Let $`v_{i}`$ indicate whether
stage $`i`$ passes. For each strict execution edge $`e`$, $`w_{e}`$ is
its weight and $`q_{e}`$ indicates verified progress. Let $`m_{j}`$
indicate whether eligible milestone $`j`$ is reached. The three direct
metrics are

|     |                               |                                                                                                       |     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{TSR}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}v_{i}}{K},`$                                                      |     | (1) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{WGP}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{e\in E_{\mathrm{exec}}}w_{e}q_{e}}{\sum_{e\in E_{\mathrm{exec}}}w_{e}},`$ |     | (2) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{VMP}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{J}m_{j}}{J}.`$                                                      |     | (3) |

TSR is the fraction of planned stages that pass; unreached stages remain
in its denominator. WGP is the weighted fraction of strict graph edges
supported by verified progress. VMP tracks eligible item or tool
milestones observed before a chain ends. It captures partial progress,
not full completion. We report all three metrics for each target
condition and compare paired runs.
Appendices [C](#A3 "Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
and [D.6](#A4.SS6 "D.6 Statistical and diagnostic reporting ‣ Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
give the verifier and reporting rules.

### 3.4 Benchmark Instantiation

MC-EvoBench implements this framework in Minecraft with a fixed task
catalog, verifiers, probe profiles, and observation interface. A change
to any of these components defines a new benchmark version. The same
evaluation can therefore test different ways of storing experience, such
as textual memories, skill libraries, prompts, or model updates, under a
shared task and evidence specification.

grouped by method family. All entries are measured and reported as TSR /
WGP / VMP in percent; the final group is the weighted average over all
12 chains.

#### 3.4.1 Frozen Catalog and Probe Families

The catalog contains 80 tasks, 111 state nodes, 369 graph edges, 19
registered chains, 12 general profiles, and 3 paired-transfer profiles.
Its 19 chains include 12 primary evaluation chains and 7 calibration or
probe chains. Tasks span building, survival, exploration, and combat.
Long chains test execution across many prerequisites. Short probes test
local transfer that an early failure in a long chain could hide. The
probes use catalog tasks and the same verifier rules.
Appendices [F](#A6 "Appendix F Complete Benchmark Suite ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
and [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Environment profiles and controlled resources ‣ Appendix A Minecraft Environment Settings ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
list the tasks, chains, and profiles.

The three probe families and their budgets are listed in
Table [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Frozen transfer probes and source exposure ‣ Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
of
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Frozen transfer probes and source exposure ‣ Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
In each family, related and target chains share a dependency pattern but
end with a different object or tool. This lets us test transfer while
keeping the required preparation steps. Each stage has a 450-step cap.
After early termination, a new episode starts until the family budget is
used.

#### 3.4.2 Environment and Observation Interface

Paired-transfer runs use public world seed 31, an empty target
inventory, and one of three fixed environment profiles
(Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Environment profiles and controlled resources ‣ Appendix A Minecraft Environment Settings ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents"));
direct-capability runs use the seeds and per-stage profiles in
Table [F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Detailed direct capability results ‣ Appendix F Complete Benchmark Suite ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
Profiles set time, weather, spawn, clearance, and public resources. They
do not provide target items, routes, private coordinates, or verifier
state. The agent must observe and collect resources through interaction.
Each target condition starts with a world and inventory reset; only the
declared agent artifact can transfer. The agent sees normal
observations, while the graph, verifier rules, diagnostics, and hidden
coordinates remain unavailable.
Appendices [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Observation access and normalized evidence ‣ Appendix A Minecraft Environment Settings ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
and [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Predicate-based task evaluation ‣ Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
detail these access rules and verifier checks.

## 4 Experimental Results

We report two complementary views of the benchmark. The direct
capability matrix measures immediate performance across the registered
catalog without a source–target transfer claim. The paired probes then
test whether a declared source artifact changes behavior on a later
target after the world is reset. Keeping these views separate
distinguishes basic execution ability from experience-driven
improvement.

| Probe family | Target-condition means        |                               |                               |
| ------------ | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
|              | TSR (N/R/U/S)                 | WGP (N/R/U/S)                 | VMP (N/R/U/S)                 |
| Wood species | 0.400 / 0.400 / 0.200 / 0.500 | 0.360 / 0.400 / 0.200 / 0.480 | 0.400 / 0.400 / 0.200 / 0.500 |
| Wooden tool  | 0.320 / 0.200 / 0.160 / 0.240 | 0.225 / 0.150 / 0.100 / 0.167 | 0.560 / 0.367 / 0.333 / 0.467 |
| Stone tool   | 0.150 / 0.050 / 0.025 / 0.075 | 0.082 / 0.021 / 0.010 / 0.031 | 0.533 / 0.200 / 0.100 / 0.300 |

Table 3: Paired transfer results for the three probe families. Values
are target-condition means over five matched seeds; each cell lists
no-prior (N), related (R), unrelated (U), and shuffled (S) conditions in
that order. TSR, WGP, and VMP measure stage completion, graph progress,
and verified milestone progress, respectively, after the target world is
reset.

### 4.1 Evaluation Setup

The paired evaluation uses three probe families: wood-species crafting,
wooden-tool transfer, and stone-tool transfer. Each family uses five
paired agent seeds and four target conditions: no prior, related
experience, unrelated experience, and shuffled related experience. Every
target starts from the same world and inventory state for its family.
Only the declared agent artifact may cross the source–target boundary.
We report TSR, WGP, and VMP as defined in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Paired Protocol and Metrics ‣ 3 MC-EvoBench Framework and Benchmark Design ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
Source exposure is matched within each family; planner calls and token
usage are recorded separately because equal environment exposure does
not imply equal computation.

### 4.2 Direct Capability Matrix

The direct matrix covers 12 primary evaluation chains (five
core-progression, four catalog-transfer, and three diversity) and nine
direct configurations, each evaluated with three seeds. Each cell in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.4 Benchmark Instantiation ‣ 3 MC-EvoBench Framework and Benchmark Design ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
averages TSR / WGP / VMP over the chains in a partition; the final
columns weight the partitions by their sizes (5/4/3), and Appendix
Table [F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Detailed direct capability results ‣ Appendix F Complete Benchmark Suite ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
gives per-chain scores. These runs measure direct capability rather than
transfer; ExpeL ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)) has one separately
marked report per chain and is excluded from these aggregates.

Controller-based execution clearly outperforms planner-backed execution.
STEVE-1 ([Lifshitz et al., 2023](#bib.bib15)) and the controller-only
JARVIS-1 ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)) and Optimus-1 ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)) variants reach average TSR/WGP/VMP of 8.4/6.4/25.5,
7.5/5.5/25.0, and 8.1/6.1/25.4, with the largest margins on the core and
catalog-transfer partitions, where progress requires several dependent
actions. The no-op baseline and the GPT-planned JARVIS-1 remain at the
execution floor, confirming that the benchmark separates active task
solving from background behavior. No planner dominates all three
metrics: DeepSeek gives the highest average TSR for both JARVIS-1 (2.8)
and Optimus-1 (4.9), whereas the highest VMP comes from DeepSeek for
JARVIS-1 (6.0) but from GLM for Optimus-1 (12.5). The official VPT
([Baker et al., 2022](#bib.bib18)) foundation weights improve over the
STEVE-1 checkpoint (average VMP 10.4 versus 3.2) but remain below the
controller variants.

### 4.3 Paired Transfer Results

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
reports mean target scores in the order no-prior / related / unrelated /
shuffled. The study contains 105 source and target role reports in
total, with 60 target reports contributing to the four-condition
comparison.

For wood-species crafting, related experience gives scores close to no
prior. The shuffled control scores at least as high on TSR and WGP. For
wooden-tool and stone-tool transfer, related experience scores below no
prior on all three metrics. On the stone-tool probe, related TSR, WGP,
and VMP are 0.050, 0.021, and 0.200, compared with 0.150, 0.082, and
0.533 for no prior.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 4.4 Paired Contrasts and Uncertainty

For each direct metric, let $`M_{0}`$, $`M_{R}`$, $`M_{U}`$, and
$`M_{S}`$ denote the no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled target
scores. We report the related-source change $`\Delta R=M_{R}-M_{0}`$.
For completeness,
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Paired Contrasts and Uncertainty ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
also reports the adjusted contrast

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathrm{GATG}=M_{R}-\frac{1}{2}(M_{U}+M_{S}).
       ```                                            |     |

GATG is used here only as a descriptive paired contrast; TSR, WGP, and
VMP remain the benchmark’s direct metrics. Intervals are two-sided 95%
Student-$`t`$ intervals over the five paired seeds.

| Metric | Wood species |       |                   | Wooden tool  |        |                   | Stone tool   |       |                   |
| ------ | ------------ | ----- | ----------------- | ------------ | ------ | ----------------- | ------------ | ----- | ----------------- |
|        | $`\Delta R`$ | GATG  | 95% CI            | $`\Delta R`$ | GATG   | 95% CI            | $`\Delta R`$ | GATG  | 95% CI            |
| TSR    | 0.000        | 0.050 | \[-0.723, 0.823\] | -0.120       | 0.000  | \[-0.152, 0.152\] | -0.100       | 0.000 | \[-0.095, 0.095\] |
| WGP    | 0.040        | 0.060 | \[-0.718, 0.838\] | -0.075       | 0.017  | \[-0.132, 0.166\] | -0.062       | 0.000 | \[-0.039, 0.039\] |
| VMP    | 0.000        | 0.050 | \[-0.723, 0.823\] | -0.193       | -0.033 | \[-0.248, 0.181\] | -0.333       | 0.000 | \[-0.380, 0.380\] |

Table 4: Paired transfer contrasts over five matched seeds. Columns are
grouped by probe family and report the related-source change
($`\Delta R`$), the diagnostic GATG contrast, and its two-sided 95%
Student-$`t`$ confidence interval. GATG is not an additional benchmark
metric.

Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Paired Contrasts and Uncertainty ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
separates the direct related-source change from the control-adjusted
contrast. Relative to no prior, related experience improves only WGP on
the wood-species probe ($`\Delta R=+0.040`$); TSR and VMP are unchanged.
The two tool-transfer probes show negative changes on all three metrics,
with the largest decrease in VMP for stone-tool transfer
($`\Delta R=-0.333`$). After adjusting for the unrelated and shuffled
controls, the wood-species probe retains a small positive GATG on TSR,
WGP, and VMP ($`+0.050`$, $`+0.060`$, and $`+0.050`$). The wooden-tool
probe is mixed: GATG is near zero for TSR and slightly positive for WGP,
but negative for VMP. All reported confidence intervals include zero,
and the intervals are wide because they are estimated from five matched
seeds.

### 4.6 Failure Stages, Seed Variation, and Scope

In the failure-stage audit of the 57 direct-matrix reports per
configuration
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.5 Source Cost and Run Records ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")a),
attrition concentrates in the first crafting steps: of the 42 reports
that include wood collection, the three controller variants bring 20–23
to plank crafting, at most 14 to sticks, and at most 2 to the crafting
table, while the Optimus-3 ([Li et al., 2025a](#bib.bib19)) action path
never passes the initial wood stage. A low final score can therefore
reflect an early execution bottleneck rather than the failure of a later
capability, which remains unobserved. Per-seed effects
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.5 Source Cost and Run Records ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")b–c)
vary most for wood species, where the small positive mean GATG
($`+0.050`$) is driven by a single seed ($`+1.0`$) and falls to
$`-0.19`$ without it; the tool probes vary less and have GATG means near
zero. All three intervals cross zero, consistent with
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Paired Contrasts and Uncertainty ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").

Taken together, the direct matrix measures immediate capability rather
than transfer, and the paired probes should be read against its low
execution floor. Under the current public instances, seeds, budgets, and
reference method, related experience does not produce a stable positive
transfer effect; this does not rule out gains under a different agent,
artifact, task distribution, or source budget.
Appendices [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Stage records and evidence organization ‣ Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents"),
[D.6](#A4.SS6 "D.6 Statistical and diagnostic reporting ‣ Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents"),
and [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Configured parameters and replication ‣ Appendix E Agent implementations ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
give the stage records, paired-reporting rules, and configuration fields
needed to reproduce these comparisons.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced MC-EvoBench, a controlled Minecraft benchmark for auditing
whether experience yields durable and transferable embodied
capabilities. Its task-state graph, stage-level verifiers, and paired
reset-target protocol with matched control sources separate capability
change from carried-over resources, unequal exposure, and early
execution failures. In the reference study, controller-based agents
clearly outperform planner-backed variants, yet the reference method
gains no stable target benefit from related experience: the only
positive contrast, on wood species, is driven by a single seed, and all
intervals include zero even though related sources earn more verified
progress and, on the longer probes, more computation. Most runs also end
before crafting sticks, leaving later capabilities unobserved. These
conclusions are limited to the tested agents, probes, seeds, and
budgets; retention, composition, stronger agents, and more seeds are
natural next steps.

### AI use statement

We used generative AI tools for English translation, language editing,
shortening text, and LaTeX formatting. We did not use AI to generate
data, run experiments, or draw the final conclusions. The authors
checked all citations, equations, experimental settings, and results.
They reviewed all AI-assisted text and take full responsibility for the
paper.

### Ethics statement

This work evaluates agents in a virtual Minecraft environment. It does
not involve human participants, personal data, or physical-world
experiments. We use environment states and agent interaction traces to
measure task execution and experience transfer. Any released code, task
definitions, assets, and logs will follow their applicable licenses and
include documentation for reproduction. The results apply to the tested
methods, tasks, environments, and budgets. They do not establish that
these agents are safe or capable in real-world settings.

### Reproducibility statement

Section [3](#S3 "3 MC-EvoBench Framework and Benchmark Design ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
defines the task-state graph, source–target protocol, and metrics.
Section [4](#S4 "4 Experimental Results ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
reports the reference results.
Appendices [A](#A1 "Appendix A Minecraft Environment Settings ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")–[C](#A3 "Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
give the environment profiles, task and chain definitions, verifier
rules, stage records, and metric calculations.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
describes resets, source budgets, target roles, seeds, artifact
transfer, and paired reporting.
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
gives the memory formats, prompts, example configuration, evaluation
procedure, and reproduction commands. Run records include the fixed task
and verifier settings, seeds, source exposure, artifact identities, and
stage evidence needed to check the reported scores.

## Appendix A Minecraft Environment Settings

MC-EvoBench evaluates whether interaction experience can improve
subsequent embodied execution. Its experimental unit joins a source
experience, a persistent agent artifact, and a separately initialized
target evaluation. This appendix specifies the environment, task
construction, verification, experimental protocol, agent interfaces,
task suite, and reproducibility materials.

### A.1 Game world and interaction interface

The primary environment is Minecraft 1.16.5 through MineRL, with a
custom survival specification named MCBenchHumanSurvival-v0. It extends
the HumanSurvival environment with observations for inventory, local
resources, world conditions, and task events. The agent interacts with
the game through an adapter, while a separate evaluator converts the
environment response into a normalized observation snapshot. This
separation supports a common task definition across agents with
different planning and control architectures.

The native control interface consists of movement, camera rotation,
attack, use, and inventory operations. Camera commands change pitch and
yaw; the meaning of attack and use depends on whether the agent is
interacting with the world or an inventory interface. These environment
actions produce the observations used for task verification.
Text-conditioned controllers translate a task instruction into this
action interface. A programmatic agent may use a different bridge, in
which case its action granularity is reported with the method settings
in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Agent implementations ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").

Table A1. Interaction and observation interfaces. The evaluator consumes
the evidence needed by a task; an agent consumes the modalities exposed
by its declared adapter.

| Component                  | Representation                                    | Role                                                                  |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Visual input               | First-person RGB frame                            | Scene perception and low-level control                                |
| Movement                   | Forward, back, left, right; jump, sneak, sprint   | Navigation and locomotion                                             |
| Camera                     | Relative pitch and yaw                            | Viewpoint and interaction targeting                                   |
| Interaction                | Attack, use, drop, inventory, hotbar selection    | Resource collection, construction, and item manipulation              |
| Inventory and equipment    | Item counts; normalized equipped-item names       | Agent context when exposed; task verification                         |
| Local resource evidence    | Ray observation and block-count grid              | Structured perception or evaluator evidence, according to the adapter |
| World and mission evidence | Time, light, survival state, entity-kill counters | Event verification and execution diagnostics                          |

![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.13829v1/fig/environment.png)

Figure A1. The task specification connects initialization, agent
execution, and evaluation. World configuration fixes the problem
instance. Agent inputs follow the selected interface, while success is
evaluated from environment evidence. Persistent experience crosses
source and target runs through the artifact boundary defined in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").

### A.2 Observation access and normalized evidence

The catalog distinguishes native_perception and structured_state
observation sources. Each source records a path, its primary or
diagnostic role, its interpretation, and an access declaration.
Inventory, equipment, and basic survival measurements are examples of
declared agent-visible sources. Local block counts, mission flags, kill
counters, and world-light diagnostics are classified as structured
evidence. RGB-based and structured-state methods therefore remain
distinguishable even when they share the same task verifier.

At runtime, the snapshot groups observations into inventory, equipment,
player statistics, counters, flags, raw observations, and environment
metadata. Equipment names are normalized across MineRL representations,
and raw entity-kill observations can populate the corresponding
normalized counter. The evaluator preserves the raw channel alongside
the normalized value, which makes it possible to trace a predicate back
to its observation source. The actual model inputs are determined by the
adapter;
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Agent implementations ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
describes the built-in interfaces.

The local block grid spans offsets from $`(-3,-2,-3)`$ to $`(3,2,3)`$
around the player, giving a $`7\times 5\times 7`$ observation volume.
The ray channel supplies a block identity and distance. Grid counts
support local structure checks; ray observations support direct resource
visibility. Profile-provided resource markers describe the configured
scene and serve as diagnostics. The coal-discovery predicate uses coal
observed in the ray channel or local block grid.

### A.3 Environment profiles and controlled resources

An environment profile specifies a world seed, time of day, weather,
initial inventory, and optional placement metadata. The benchmark
includes 12 general environment profiles, all with empty initial
inventories. Four forest profiles provide progression, daytime,
nighttime, and dusk settings. Controlled-resource profiles place scarce
materials near the spawn so that a finite evaluation budget can probe
tool preparation, mining, collection, and downstream use. Ore is a world
object that the agent must interact with.

Table A2. General environment profile registry. Codes are used in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Complete Benchmark Suite ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
Seeds are profile defaults; an experiment can override them explicitly.
All entries initialize an empty inventory.

| Code | Profile                     | Seed | Time / controlled setting                              |
| ---- | --------------------------- | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| P01  | forest_progression          | 42   | Tick 1,000; time progresses                            |
| P02  | forest_day                  | 7    | Tick 1,000; daylight                                   |
| P03  | forest_night                | 11   | Tick 14,000; hostile spawning enabled                  |
| P04  | forest_dusk                 | 9    | Tick 12,000; dusk                                      |
| P05  | fixed_coal_shaft            | 21   | Exposed coal; radius 4; catalog y-band 73–74           |
| P06  | fixed_iron_shaft            | 21   | Iron; radius 4; catalog y-band 70–71                   |
| P07  | fixed_gold_shaft            | 21   | Gold; radius 4; catalog y-band 70–71                   |
| P08  | fixed_redstone_shaft        | 21   | Redstone; radius 4; catalog y-band 70–71               |
| P09  | fixed_lapis_shaft           | 21   | Lapis; radius 4; catalog y-band 70–71                  |
| P10  | fixed_diamond_shaft         | 21   | Diamond; radius 4; catalog y-band 70–71                |
| P11  | fixed_emerald_shaft         | 21   | Emerald; radius 4; catalog y-band 70–71                |
| P12  | fixed_ore_progression_shaft | 21   | Seven-resource gallery; radius 6; catalog y-band 70–71 |

Resource placement is specified relative to the configured or actual
spawn, as recorded in the profile. The multi-resource gallery contains
coal, iron, gold, redstone, lapis, diamond, and emerald. These local
arrangements standardize access to task materials; they measure
execution under controlled resource availability. The source files
retain block placement, facing direction, resource identity, and
allowed-task metadata.

The paired-transfer configurations use three additional profiles: a
mixed wood-species grove, an oak grove, and a stone gallery. They use
world seed 31, daylight, clear weather, disabled spawning, and an empty
initial inventory. Their nearby resources support paired source and
target tasks with comparable access conditions. Related and unrelated
source content, interaction budgets, and target substitutions are
specified together in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").

### A.4 State continuity within a task chain

The chain specification selects either a task-level or chain-level
profile policy. Under the task-level policy, the runner selects each
task’s profile; with the default per-stage reset setting, a profile
change causes an environment reset. Under the chain-level policy, one
selected profile governs the chain. Consecutive stages that remain in
the same environment can reuse world resources and inventory, making
state continuity an explicit part of chain evaluation.

This within-chain continuity is separate from the source-to-target
boundary. A target transfer evaluation starts from its prescribed
environment state and receives only the permitted persistent artifact. A
tool retained between two stages changes their execution conditions; a
tool reconstructed after a target reset provides evidence about
execution under the retained agent state. The protocol records these two
situations separately.

## Appendix B Task Construction and Composition

### B.1 Task specification and benchmark coverage

A task is a compact executable contract: an identifier, an instruction,
a domain, a step budget, an environment profile, a success
specification, and observation-source declarations. Instructions
describe ordinary Minecraft objectives such as collecting a resource or
crafting a tool. The success specification supplies the measurable
endpoint. Keeping these fields together allows the same task to be
placed in a short probe, a longer chain, or an independent evaluation
without redefining its meaning.

The task catalog contains 80 tasks across building, survival,
exploration, and combat. The domain counts are 40, 26, 7, and 7,
respectively. The accompanying graph contains 111 state nodes and 369
edges. Its composition rules connect resource acquisition, crafting,
tool use, environmental conditions, and high-level events.
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Complete Benchmark Suite ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
provides the complete task and chain definitions; the machine-readable
tables retain the original instructions and predicates.

Table B1. Catalog partitions and their execution denominators. A task
identifier can occur more than once in a chain or across chains. Stage
occurrences are therefore counted separately from distinct task
membership.

| Partition                | Declared tasks | Chains | Stage occurrences | Purpose                                               |
| ------------------------ | -------------- | ------ | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Core progression         | 33             | 5      | 71                | Resource, tool-tier, survival, and combat progression |
| Transfer                 | 31             | 4      | 50                | Item, recipe, and schema substitutions                |
| Supplementary diversity  | 16             | 3      | 19                | Breadth of collection and resource interaction        |
| Calibration and probe    | 0              | 7      | 51                | Execution and verifier checks                         |
| Primary evaluation total | 80             | 12     | 140               | Core, transfer, and diversity combined                |

The first three partitions define the primary evaluation suite. The
calibration partition reuses task definitions for engineering checks and
is reported separately. This organization supplies both a stable
comparison set and a small set of diagnostic entry points. The
task-membership split describes the catalog taxonomy; shared
prerequisites can still recur in the executable chains.

### B.2 Task–state graph

Let $`\mathcal{T}`$ denote task nodes and $`\mathcal{S}`$ state nodes. A
state represents an item, tool, location, environmental condition,
player condition, structure, entity event, or abstract group. Directed
typed edges specify how a task relates to these states. The resulting
graph is

|     |                              |                                                                                                                                                                            |     |       |
| --- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ----- |
|     | $`\displaystyle G`$          | $`\displaystyle=(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{E}),`$                                                                                                                   |     | (B.1) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{E}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{req}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{prod}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cons}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{enable}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{abs}}.`$ |     |       |

Table B2. Edge types in the released catalog. Counts describe graph
definitions, before expansion into repeated stage occurrences.

| Relation     | Direction     | Count | Meaning                                            |
| ------------ | ------------- | ----- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| requires     | State to task | 117   | Hard prerequisite for ordered composition          |
| produces     | Task to state | 81    | Declared output of a completed task                |
| consumes     | Task to state | 28    | Resource used by the task                          |
| enables      | State to task | 15    | Soft capability relation for probe design          |
| abstracts_to | Node to group | 128   | Semantic grouping across concrete tasks and states |

The relations in
Eq. [B.1](#A2.E1 "In B.2 Task–state graph ‣ Appendix B Task Construction and Composition ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
are listed in
Table [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Task–state graph ‣ Appendix B Task Construction and Composition ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
The first three define the execution paths used in weighted graph
progress. Soft enabling and abstraction edges organize capability
relationships without contributing to this execution score. This makes
the graph useful at two levels: concrete dependencies support
composition, while abstract groups organize transfer questions across
items or recipes.

![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.13829v1/fig/task_graph.png)

Figure B1. A catalog fragment links log collection to plank production.
Task nodes and state nodes have distinct shapes; edge labels retain
their direction and quantity. The graph describes a declared dependency
structure. Runtime observations and task predicates determine which
execution stages actually pass.

### B.3 Ordered chain compilation

A chain stores an ordered task sequence, initial symbolic states, an
environment profile, and a profile policy. The compiler traverses the
sequence and extracts five paths for every occurrence: hard
prerequisites, produced resources, consumed resources, soft enabling
relations, and abstraction relations. Repeated task identifiers become
distinct compiled stages, so their positions and local context remain
available to the evaluator.

The default compiler checks prerequisite presence in the evolving
symbolic state set. An optional strict-quantity mode also checks
declared resource counts before consuming and producing them. Let
$`q_{j}(s)`$ be the symbolic availability of state $`s`$ before stage
$`j`$. In the strict mode, a stage requires sufficient declared counts,
after which its resource bookkeeping follows

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       q_{j+1}(s)=q_{j}(s)-c_{j}(s)+p_{j}(s),
       ```                                     |     | (B.2) |

where $`c_{j}`$ and $`p_{j}`$ are the stage’s consumption and production
counts. Initial symbolic states seed this calculation; they do not grant
physical inventory. The simulator independently realizes movement,
mining, crafting, and resource use.

This separation is useful when constructing a benchmark: a chain can be
checked for intended ordering before a game is launched, and its
execution can then be evaluated from observations.
Equation [B.2](#A2.E2 "In B.3 Ordered chain compilation ‣ Appendix B Task Construction and Composition ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
describes symbolic bookkeeping only. The compilerś output also gives
each stage a fixed metric context, with graph weights fixed by the
planned chain before execution.

### B.4 Composition patterns

Resource progression chains connect acquisition to increasingly
demanding use. For example, the ore progression chain moves through wood
preparation, basic tools, stone tools, ore collection, smelting, and
higher-tier mining. Cross-domain chains join heterogeneous endpoints:
locating coal, obtaining fuel, creating illumination, building shelter,
and remaining alive, or preparing a weapon before a combat event.
Transfer chains substitute wood species, tool recipes, or item roles
while retaining comparable dependency patterns.

The task suite also includes short probes. These isolate resource
collection or limited crafting sequences, helping distinguish an early
execution bottleneck from a long-horizon planning requirement. A short
probe and a long chain answer different questions, even when they
contain the same task identifier. Their sequence, start state, budget,
and profile policy accompany their scores.

A completed possession task establishes its predicate at that stage. If
the same item remains in inventory, a later occurrence with the same
predicate may pass immediately. The ordered stage record makes this
behavior explicit: initial-state passes have zero action steps, while
newly acquired items appear in the observed state transition.
Composition is consequently described through stage outcomes and state
continuity, with experience transfer assessed by the reset protocol in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").

### B.5 Extending the catalog

A new task can be added by defining its instruction and measurable
endpoint, identifying the required observation channels, selecting an
environment profile, and attaching its graph relations. A new chain then
specifies an ordered list of existing or new task identifiers.
Compilation checks the declared dependency order, and an execution check
verifies that the configured environment exposes the evidence required
by its predicates.

The reusable components are the task contract, graph relations, profile
registry, and runner interface. A method’s planner, retrieval rule, or
memory format remains outside the task definition. This allows a future
agent to implement a different experience representation while being
evaluated against the same target objectives and evidence rules.

## Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics

### C.1 Predicate-based task evaluation

MC-EvoBench evaluates success from environment observations. A task
contains a conjunction of predicates, with optional disjunctive
subexpressions. Inventory thresholds check resource or item possession;
equipment predicates accept an item in a specified slot; counters
capture events such as an entity defeat; snapshot comparisons read a
named observation field. These primitives cover both simple item goals
and objectives that combine player state with local environmental
conditions.

Table C1. Supported predicate families and their measurement roles.

| Predicate family      | Accepted evidence                               | Example                                           |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Inventory threshold   | Named item count at or above a threshold        | At least four oak planks                          |
| Equipment equality    | Normalized item in the specified equipment slot | Stone sword in the main hand                      |
| Counter threshold     | Observed event count                            | At least one zombie defeated                      |
| Player-stat threshold | Named player measurement                        | Positive life or health                           |
| Snapshot comparison   | Named path, comparison operator, and value      | Observed coal-ore indicator at least one          |
| Flag membership       | Flag produced by the configured event logic     | A mission state supported by its observation rule |
| Disjunction           | At least one successful child predicate         | Item in inventory or equipped                     |

A snapshot-path comparison fails when its required path is absent.
Inventory and counter thresholds use zero for a missing count. The
diagnostic record stores the predicate and its observed value, making
the distinction between a satisfied condition and unavailable supporting
evidence inspectable. Item possession is measured directly from
environment observations.

The evaluator checks the initial snapshot before requesting an action.
If all predicates already hold, the stage passes with zero steps.
Otherwise, it checks after each environment transition until success, a
mission failure, environment termination, or budget exhaustion. A stage
limit is the smaller of its catalog budget and any configured cap. The
normal chain runner stops at the first non-passing stage, preserving the
distinction between the observed prefix and unattempted suffix.

### C.2 Mission events

Four mission-event definitions extend the basic predicates with
observation-derived conditions. Their triggers combine local perception,
lighting, elapsed time, and entity events. Event evaluation can attach a
normalized flag or counter to the snapshot, after which the ordinary
task verifier reads the corresponding evidence. This approach keeps
event semantics shared between the runner and the task specification.

Table C2. Mission-event rules. Thresholds are taken from the catalog.
The shelter rule is a local structure-and-light criterion; the night
rule measures a defined survival interval.

| Event                   | Trigger                                                                                                              | Endpoint                              |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Coal source observed    | Coal ore appears in the ray channel or local block grid                                                              | Observed resource discovery           |
| Lit shelter observed    | At least one local torch; at least 60 non-air blocks; effective light at least 7; sky light at most 7 or sky blocked | Local sheltered and lit condition     |
| Night interval survived | Player alive; elapsed time at least 1,800 ticks; final time in the night window from 12,000 to 24,000                | Survival over the configured interval |
| Zombie defeat observed  | Normalized zombie counter or raw zombie-kill count at least one                                                      | Observed combat event                 |

For survive_first_night, the runner also derives night_survived from
player survival and elapsed time reaching the effective stage limit.
This additional path uses the total-time difference when available; its
world-time fallback also requires a night endpoint. Thus the effective
interval follows a configured stage cap, while
Table [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Mission events ‣ Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
specifies the catalog event rule. Survival, shelter, and combat events
include a player-death failure condition. Event records preserve the
evidence that caused a terminal decision, so later analysis can connect
a stage outcome to the underlying world measurement.

### C.3 Stage records and evidence organization

Each stage record identifies the task occurrence, terminal status,
action-step count, and failed predicates. Its diagnostics include start
and final snapshots, declared observation sources, actual predicate
values, mission evidence, and the compiled graph paths. The chain report
retains the planned stage count and planned graph weight even when
execution stops early.

Table C3. Terminal statuses and their interpretation in chain
aggregation.

| Status             | Interpretation                                       | Contribution to passed-stage numerator           |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| passed             | All success predicates hold                          | One                                              |
| failed             | A configured mission failure is observed             | Zero                                             |
| terminated         | The environment ends before success                  | Zero                                             |
| timeout            | The effective stage limit is exhausted               | Zero                                             |
| budget_exhausted   | A smaller remaining chain/source budget is exhausted | Zero                                             |
| Unattempted suffix | Earlier stopping prevents execution                  | Zero, with missing execution recorded separately |

This record supports analysis at several resolutions. A chain score
summarizes completed requirements; stage records locate its execution
breakpoint; start and final states describe resource changes; and
optional action traces support a finer behavioral account. These
resolutions share the same task identity and sequence position.

### C.4 Task success rate and weighted graph progress

For chain $`c`$, let $`L_{c}`$ be its number of planned stage
occurrences and $`y_{cj}`$ indicate whether occurrence $`j`$ passes.
Task success rate is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathrm{TSR}=\frac{1}{L_{c}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{c}}y_{cj}.
       ```                                                    |     | (C.1) |

In
Eq. [C.1](#A3.E1 "In C.4 Task success rate and weighted graph progress ‣ Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents"),
unattempted stages remain in the planned denominator. At split level,
the aggregate pools passed occurrences and planned occurrences across
the included chains. This weights every planned occurrence equally,
while completed-chain counts offer a complementary measure of end-to-end
execution.

For chain $`c`$, let $`E_{\mathrm{exec},c}`$ be its strict execution
edges, formed by the requires, produces, and consumes relations. Let
$`w_{e}`$ be the edge weight and $`q_{e}`$ indicate whether the
corresponding verified stage contributes. Edge weights default to one
when unspecified. Weighted graph progress is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathrm{WGP}=\frac{\sum_{e\in E_{\mathrm{exec},c}}w_{e}q_{e}}{\sum_{e\in E_{\mathrm{exec},c}}w_{e}}.
``` |  | (C.2) |

In
Eq. [C.2](#A3.E2 "In C.4 Task success rate and weighted graph progress ‣ Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents"),
an edge is credited when its corresponding verified stage contributes.
Shared resources can appear in several stage paths, and each occurrence
contributes its local edge weight. Split WGP pools completed and planned
edge weights across chains. A chain with no planned execution-edge
weight falls back to TSR. Together, TSR and WGP summarize stage
completion and its execution structure using fixed planned denominators.

### C.5 Milestone and efficiency diagnostics

Verified milestone progress (VMP) describes observed acquisition of
graph-linked items or tools. For each reported stage, the metric
extracts item/tool states from its execution paths and assigns each
state the largest included edge-count threshold. A state is eligible if
the first recorded snapshot is below its threshold; it is credited if a
later recorded stage-start or stage-final snapshot reaches the
threshold. The score is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{VMP}=\frac{\text{eligible states reaching their thresholds}}{\text{eligible states}},
``` |  | (C.3) |

Equation [C.3](#A3.E3 "In C.5 Milestone and efficiency diagnostics ‣ Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
returns zero when the eligible set is empty. The associated eligible
count is part of its interpretation. Because this set follows the
reported prefix, VMP is used as a local acquisition diagnostic alongside
the fixed-denominator TSR and WGP endpoints. A task passes when its
success predicates hold.

Efficiency summaries include environment steps, stage budgets, steps per
passed stage, and observed deaths. Resource-use diagnostics identify
consumed items whose inventory decreases during a non-passing stage.
This provides a traceable signal of material expenditure associated with
unsuccessful execution. Recovery events require an explicit adapter
record and can then be aligned with stage transitions.

### C.6 Verification examples

The task craft_planks requires at least four oak planks. The objective
is therefore satisfied by the corresponding inventory count. For
craft_stone_sword, the catalog accepts a stone sword either in inventory
or in the main hand, matching the game’s distinction between carrying
and equipping a tool. The coal-discovery task uses observed coal in a
ray or grid channel; the subsequent coal-collection task checks the
collected item.

These examples illustrate why the task contract separates an
instruction, its observation sources, and its terminal predicate. The
instruction gives the agent a goal, the observation contract defines the
evidence channels, and the predicate fixes the endpoint. The same
decomposition supports independently checking an item goal, a temporal
objective, or a cross-domain chain through explicit predicates.

## Appendix D Evaluation protocol

### D.1 Experience, artifact, and target evaluation

MC-EvoBench separates capability measurement from the experience that
may change an agent. A paired evaluation first measures a target with
the base agent, then measures the same target with an artifact produced
through a specified source curriculum. The artifact may contain updated
parameters, memory, a skill library, or another declared persistent
representation. Its identity and provenance define the agent state being
evaluated. This interface accommodates different adaptation mechanisms
while keeping the target task and its verifier fixed.

At the source-to-target boundary, the target world and inventory are
reset. Only the frozen method-produced artifact crosses this boundary.
Consequently, tools, blocks, completed constructions, and resource
inventories accumulated during source interaction do not supply target
progress. In the supplied memory configuration, source interaction uses
read_write memory and target evaluation uses read_only memory. Each
target role constructs a fresh agent and environment; persistent source
experience is loaded from its declared artifact.

Within a compiled chain, stages execute in order and preserve the
environment state permitted by the chain profile. The runner stops at
the first non-passing stage. The transfer probes use one chain-level
profile throughout an episode. Source episodes can restart to complete
their interaction budget, as described in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Frozen transfer probes and source exposure ‣ Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
These distinct boundaries preserve sequential task dependencies within
an episode and isolate learned experience across evaluations.

![\[Uncaptioned image\]](2610.13829v1/fig/protocol.png)

Figure D1. Each source condition produces its own artifact from the same
base agent. Target evaluations share task, world, budget, and seed
settings. At the boundary, the world, inventory, and transient agent
state are reset while the declared persistent artifact is retained.

### D.2 Paired target roles and controls

Each probe and replicate defines three source roles and four target
roles. All four target roles use the same target task sequence,
verifier, environment profile, world seed, stage limits, and agent seed.
They differ in the artifact supplied to the agent.

Table D1. Target roles and the question addressed by each source
condition.

|  Target role |  Artifact supplied |  Comparison supported |
|----|----|----|
|  No prior |  Base artifact without the evaluated source experience |  Initial target capability |
|  Related |  Artifact after graph-related source tasks |  Transfer from relevant experience |
|  Unrelated |  Artifact after unrelated source tasks |  Effect of generic extra experience |
|  Shuffled |  Artifact after the related task multiset in reversed order |  Sensitivity to source ordering |

The unrelated and shuffled source conditions receive the same
family-level environment-step budget as the related condition. The
shuffled source uses the identical task multiset, including repeated
tasks. Its probe explicitly allows compilation with unmet prerequisites,
making the reversed sequence executable without adding inventory or
changing success predicates. Normal runtime stopping rules still apply,
so the resulting experience can include repeated unsuccessful episodes.

The target input contract provides the natural-language instruction and
agent observation, together with the declared artifact. It reserves
graph-relation manifests, verifier predicates, verifier diagnostics, and
hidden resource coordinates for evaluation. The built-in method inputs
are detailed in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Agent implementations ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
Public resource placement defines the controlled task instance. It does
not supply target inventory items, forced success evidence, private
route hints, or scripted actions.

### D.3 Frozen transfer probes and source exposure

The protocol provides three shorter graph-chain families assembled from
catalog tasks. Shorter targets make transfer at intermediate
capabilities observable even when a long progression chain stops at an
early prerequisite. The plan freezes task sequences, resource profiles,
source–target relations, and budgets before adaptive paired evaluation.

Table D2. Transfer probe families. Source exposure is matched within
each row; the target sequence is held fixed across artifact conditions.

|  Probe family |  Related source $`\rightarrow`$ target variation |  Stages per sequence |  Source steps per condition |
|----|----|----|----|
|  Wood species |  Birch logs and planks $`\rightarrow`$ acacia logs and planks |  2 |  900 |
|  Wooden tools |  Wood preparation and wooden axe $`\rightarrow`$ wooden shovel |  5 |  2,250 |
|  Stone tools |  Wood/stone preparation and stone pickaxe $`\rightarrow`$ stone shovel |  8 |  3,600 |

The wooden-tool pair shares the log, plank, stick, and crafting-table
preparation sequence. The stone-tool pair additionally shares
wooden-pickaxe preparation and two cobblestone-mining stages. Unrelated
source sequences contain the same number of stages and use collection
tasks outside the selected production chain. The resource profiles
provide local world resources while retaining the need to acquire and
transform them through agent interaction.

The probe configuration imposes a 450-step ceiling on each stage,
retaining a lower catalog limit if one exists. The fixed-exposure source
runner is enabled by experiment.source_interaction_budget_steps. Source
exposure is measured as actual environment interactions. If a source
episode ends before its family budget is consumed, the agent receives
normal terminal feedback, the source environment resets, and interaction
resumes with the persistent method artifact. The last episode is
truncated at the remaining budget. Thus early completion or failure
changes the number of episodes without reducing the prescribed source
exposure. The source report records every episode and the total
interaction count; a final paired comparison requires all three source
conditions to consume the common budget.

### D.4 Replicates and reproducibility

The headline paired protocol uses five final agent seeds, 5100–5104.
Separate calibration checks may use at least three direct seeds, but
they are not part of the 105 role configurations or the headline
results. The replicate axis is agent randomness on a fixed controlled
world: the public world seed is 31. Fixing the world preserves the
declared spawn placement and local resource layout across conditions.
The resulting paired estimates characterize variation across agent seeds
on these controlled instances.

Run labels such as seed0 identify records; numerical world_seed and
agent_seed fields determine randomization. The runner applies the world
seed to the environment and seeds Python, NumPy, and PyTorch before
constructing the policy. Reports retain both seeds and their provenance.
Every role in a paired replicate uses the same numerical seeds, and the
same replicate list is used across conditions.

Before rollout, the launcher checks the declared resource profile
through an environment reset. Artifact manifests record identities and
paths, with SHA-256 fingerprints available for files and directory
bundles. Together, the frozen plan, explicit seeds, artifact identity,
and runtime configuration specify a reproducible comparison.

### D.5 Transfer contrasts

TSR, WGP, and VMP follow the definitions in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Success Verification and Execution Metrics ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
Let $`M_{0},M_{R},M_{U},M_{S}`$ denote a target score with no prior,
related, unrelated, and shuffled artifacts, respectively. Define each
source condition’s change from the no-prior target as

|     |                                              |     |       |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta_{c}=M_{c}-M_{0},\qquad c\in\{R,U,S\}.
       ```                                           |     | (D.1) |

The paired differences in
Eq. [D.1](#A4.E1 "In D.5 Transfer contrasts ‣ Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
are interpreted across the three direct metrics. A related-source change
is compared with both the no-prior baseline and the matched unrelated
and shuffled controls; these are contrasts over TSR, WGP, and VMP rather
than additional benchmark metrics. Target TSR is the primary channel,
while WGP and VMP provide complementary completion and acquisition
diagnostics.

### D.6 Statistical and diagnostic reporting

Compute contrasts within each matched replicate before summarizing
across seeds. Report the four target scores and paired differences for
each direct metric, with their means and sample standard deviations. The
aggregation helper also computes two-sided 95% Student-t intervals on
paired seed contrasts:

|     |                                                    |     |       |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|-------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \bar{d}\ \pm\ t_{0.975,n-1}\frac{s_{d}}{\sqrt{n}}.
       ```                                                 |     | (D.2) |

For the interval in
Eq. [D.2](#A4.E2 "In D.6 Statistical and diagnostic reporting ‣ Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents"),
$`n`$ is the number of valid pairs and $`s_{d}`$ is the sample standard
deviation of paired differences. A beneficial-transfer interpretation
requires a positive related-source change relative to the no-prior
baseline and matched controls, supported by paired uncertainty. Metric
configurations are also characterized as floor-limited, ceiling-limited,
or interior. The accompanying progress channels localize capability
acquisition across these score regimes.

Report environment steps alongside source episode counts, outcomes,
memory updates, planner calls, and token usage. Equal environment
exposure can produce different amounts of planning and updating because
episodes terminate at different points. These diagnostics characterize
the resources used to create each artifact and support computation-aware
comparisons. Per-seed target scores and source exposure remain available
alongside aggregate statistics, allowing transfer and efficiency to be
assessed together.
