````math
## Appendix E Agent implementations

### E.1 Observation and action interfaces

MC-EvoBench connects policies to a common chain runner through a policy
factory, a reset operation, and an action function. At each interaction,
the adapter supplies the task instruction and current observation and
receives a MineRL action mapping. The default prompt template is the
instruction itself. Optional callbacks provide stage status and the
number of executed steps, allowing methods with persistent memory to
update after source experience.
Table [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Observation and action interfaces ‣ Appendix E Agent implementations ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
specifies the implemented method variants and their effective inputs;
these interfaces define the observation, action, and persistent-state
conditions used in each comparison. The table documents supported
adapters; the headline reference study reported in the main paper uses
only the JARVIS-1 online extension, while the other entries do not
contribute to the paired-transfer results.

Table E1. Implemented agent interfaces. “Persistent state” identifies
information retained by the bridge for later decisions.

|  Variant |  Effective decision input |  Action and persistent state |
|----|----|----|
|  VPT |  Raw MineRL observation; instruction unused |  Released visual policy; recurrent controller state |
|  STEVE-1 / JARVIS-1 controller |  Observation and text embedding |  Released STEVE-I actions; cached prompt embeddings |
|  JARVIS online extension |  Planner: inventory, equipment, position, retrieved episodes; controller: observation and subgoal |  Local text planner with released controller; episode memory |
|  ExpeL adaptation |  Inventory, equipment, position/orientation, nearby blocks, line of sight, episodes and insights |  LLM-generated action mapping; episodes, insights and weighted rules |
|  Optimus-1 action bridge |  Screenshot file and instruction |  Released action model; direct controller execution |
|  Optimus-1 planner bridge |  Planner: screenshot and instruction; controller: screenshot and subgoal |  Local visual planner with released action model; diagnostic trace |
|  Optimus-3 action path |  Image and task-conditioned embedding |  Released MLLM, task router and action head |
|  Voyager skill bridge |  Fixed task-to-skill sequence and Mineflayer state |  Released JavaScript skills and primitives; skill files |

The STEVE-1 and JARVIS controller bridges encode text with MineCLIP and
a learned prior, cache embeddings by prompt, and reset the conditional
controller with guidance scale 6.0. VPT loads its network specification
and policy-head settings from the model file; its sampling temperature
is inherited from that file. Optimus-3 creates a task representation
when the instruction changes, then combines it with successive frames.

### E.2 Persistent experience and adaptation

The JARVIS online extension stores stage-level textual records
containing the instruction, proposed plan, dispatched controller
prompts, status, interaction count and visible-state summary. Retrieval
uses token-set Jaccard similarity between the current instruction and
each stored instruction, adds 0.15 for a successful record, and breaks
score ties in favour of newer records. Up to four positive-scoring
records condition planning. Memory retains the latest 256 records and is
written atomically. The planner returns one to six short controller
prompts; reflection produces a practical sentence capped at 500
characters. The reflection input distinguishes a proposed plan from
prompts actually dispatched and labels the state summary as the last
pre-action observation.

ExpeL uses the same episode-retrieval score and supplements episodes
with retrieved textual insights and a weighted rule list. Insight
retrieval uses lexical overlap; rule retrieval adds a weight
contribution capped at 0.10. With the configured insight limit of eight,
the planner may receive up to eight insights and eight rules. Reflection
proposes ADD, EDIT, REMOVE and AGREE operations. New rules start with
weight two; agreement and editing increment weight, while removal
decrements it. The persistent artifact records these updates alongside
episode actions. Both memory methods support read-write source
interaction and read-only target evaluation; read-only stage callbacks
suppress reflection and memory writes.

### E.3 Planning and execution cadence

The JARVIS extension plans when a new stage instruction becomes active.
It dispatches successive subgoals for fixed 120-step intervals and
retains the final subgoal for any remaining stage steps. Stage
completion invalidates the active instruction so repeated task text can
trigger a new plan. Optimus-1’s visual planner uses the same interval
rule and a JSON subgoal format. Its input is a JPEG thumbnail bounded by
384 $`\times`$ 384 pixels at quality 85. The parser filters subgoals
containing “open,” “place,” or “access” followed by a space, rewrites
punch/collect/gather to chop, and retains up to six subgoals. ExpeL
instead requests a low-level action mapping and can hold that action
across a configured number of environment steps. The 19-chain
configuration sets this hold to 32, while the factory default is one.
Its prompt also supplies explicit line-of-sight guidance for approaching
and mining visible resources.

The Voyager skill bridge follows a separate execution protocol. The
runner loads released JavaScript skills and control primitives, resets
through the Mineflayer bridge with empty inventory and equipment, and
invokes a fixed skill sequence. A configured starting position is
applied during setup. The runner checks the returned inventory for its
designated target item. Its step count denotes a bridge request, and the
implementation invokes no LLM; this execution unit is recorded
separately from MineRL interaction steps.

### E.4 Configured parameters and replication

Table [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Configured parameters and replication ‣ Appendix E Agent implementations ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
reports configuration values and the defaults used where configurations
omit a field. Planner model identifiers are recorded literally because
the standard and relay matrices select different providers. Planner
calls leave temperature unspecified. Token limits bound generated
output, and timeout or retry settings describe request handling rather
than additional environment interaction.

Table E2. Configuration values and implementation defaults. J = JARVIS
online extension; O = Optimus-1 planner bridge; E = ExpeL adaptation.

|  Component |  Configured value or applicable default |
|----|----|
|  Text-conditioned controllers |  VPT 2x.model; STEVE-1 weights and prior; guidance 6.0 for STEVE-1/JARVIS |
|  J standard / relay planner |  gpt-5.4 / gpt-5.6-sol; relay uses Responses with high reasoning effort |
|  O / E planner |  ~openai/gpt-luna-latest / gpt-5.6-sol; E uses Responses, high effort |
|  Output limit; timeout |  J: 4,096 tokens, 60 s; O: 4,096, 90 s; E: 2,048, 60 s |
|  Memory and cadence |  256 records; 4 retrieved episodes; J/O horizon 120; E insight/rule limits 8 each, action hold 32 |

The standard and relay configurations instantiate the same benchmark
roles through different planner interfaces. A reproducible method
specification records the selected matrix, policy checkpoint,
observation channels, action cadence, planner identity, and memory mode.
Replicate seeds and source budgets follow
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation protocol ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents").
These fields allow the effect of the experience mechanism to be
interpreted alongside its controller and computational settings.

## Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility

### G.1 Planning and reflection templates

The online-memory reference implementation uses two system templates.
The planning request combines the current goal, an agent-visible state
summary, and retrieved experience. It returns a small sequence of text
subgoals for the visual controller. The reflection request summarizes a
completed source episode for later retrieval.
Cards [G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Planning and reflection templates ‣ Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
and [G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Planning and reflection templates ‣ Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
specify the input–output contracts and system prompts.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The planning payload contains goal, visible_state, and
retrieved_experience. Retrieved records expose the instruction, plan,
status, and advice. The planning parser returns up to six non-empty
steps, using the task instruction as its default. Reflection receives
stage feedback together with the actually dispatched prompts, allowing
the stored advice to distinguish planned behavior from observed
execution context.

### G.2 Persistent memory representation

The artifact is a JSON object containing a record count and a list of
episode records. Each record associates a task instruction with a
proposed plan, the prompts dispatched to the controller, terminal
status, interaction count, visible state, and advice. The memory writer
keeps the latest configured number of records and replaces the artifact
atomically. Retrieval and update rules are specified in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Agent implementations ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents");
the schema below describes the fields required to inspect the stored
experience.

Table G1. Persistent memory fields and their interpretation.

|  Field |  Content |  Role in reproduction |
|----|----|----|
|  format |  Memory schema identifier |  Identifies the memory format |
|  record_count |  Number of retained records |  Checks artifact size |
|  instruction |  Task text |  Retrieval key |
|  plan |  Proposed controller prompts |  Records planner output |
|  dispatched_plan |  Prompts actually sent to the controller |  Links planning to dispatch |
|  status, steps |  Stage outcome and executed steps |  Captures feedback supplied to the method |
|  visible_state |  Agent-side state summary |  Records the reflection context |
|  advice |  Concise text retained for reuse |  Reusable experience content |

The source artifact is copied or otherwise identified before target
evaluation, and its fingerprint accompanies the target role. Read-only
target memory keeps the supplied experience fixed throughout evaluation.
This makes the artifact itself an inspectable component of a paired
comparison.

### G.3 ExpeL action and rule templates

The ExpeL adaptation uses separate system templates for selecting an
environment action and extracting reusable experience.
Cards [G.3](#A7.SS3 "G.3 ExpeL action and rule templates ‣ Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
and [G.3](#A7.SS3 "G.3 ExpeL action and rule templates ‣ Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
specify the action and reflection interfaces. The action payload
contains instruction, observation, experiences, and insights. The final
field combines insight text with retrieved rules formatted as \[ExpeL
rule weight=...\] .... This representation exposes the rule’s
persistence weight alongside its content. The observation is the
structured state summary supplied by the adapter.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The action parser accepts a mapping directly or JSON text, including a
fenced JSON response. It accepts either a nested action mapping or the
mapping itself. A singleton {"noop": true} or {"noop": 1} becomes the
adapter’s no-op marker. The action parser validates the response
mapping; task success is evaluated from environment observations.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Reflection receives the stage episode: instruction, status, steps,
actions, visible_state, visible_state_timing, and method. The state is
explicitly labeled as the last pre-action observation, and the action
list includes each returned action, including repetitions. The
reflection parser accepts insight or reflection for the insight, and
operations or rules for the operation list. It normalizes the response
into insight text and rule operations. The prompt requests up to four
rule operations per reflection.

Table G2. ExpeL persistent artifact fields. Episode records, extracted
insights, and rule-update history are stored separately.

|  Field |  Stored content |
|----|----|
|  format |  ExpeL memory schema identifier |
|  record_count, insight_count |  Sizes of the retained episode and insight lists |
|  records |  Stage episodes with action and feedback fields |
|  insights |  Whitespace-normalized reusable text |
|  rules |  Rule objects containing text and integer weight |
|  rule_events |  Normalized operations, list_full, and the resulting rules snapshot |

The artifact therefore preserves both the interaction record and the
rule state used for subsequent decisions. The loader validates the
artifact’s format identifier.

### G.4 Configuration example

Card [G.4](#A7.SS4 "G.4 Configuration example ‣ Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
gives the protocol fields from the wood-species target-after-related
configuration. It includes the selected environment, agent randomness,
memory mode, and target sequence. The complete repository file also
specifies checkpoint locations, planner settings, artifact paths, role
metadata, and output locations. Deployment paths and artifact format
identifiers are resolved through reproduction/paths.json.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The target collects acacia logs and crafts acacia planks while using the
artifact generated by the related birch source. The chain profile
remains constant within this episode. Stage limits are applied by the
runner, and task success uses the catalog predicates. The source role
uses its own task sequence and enables memory writing; all target roles
retain the same task definition.

### G.5 Evaluation algorithm

The following pseudocode summarizes the common orchestration contract.
Source interaction, artifact persistence, environment reset, and target
evaluation are separate operations. The same control flow can host
parameter updates, text memory, or executable skills, provided that the
permitted persistent state and input interface are declared.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At the task level, evaluation first observes the initial state, then
alternates action and predicate evaluation until a terminal condition is
reached. At the chain level, the runner applies the selected profile
policy and records the first non-passing stage. At the experiment level,
matched roles are combined within a seed before aggregation. These
layers align environment execution, task success, and experience
comparison at their respective units of analysis.

### G.6 Reproduction entry points

Table [G.6](#A7.SS6 "G.6 Reproduction entry points ‣ Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
identifies the small set of source components that define the benchmark.
The accompanying task and chain CSV files provide compact access to the
catalog, while the JSON source files retain the executable definitions.

Table G3. Source map for reproducing the definitions in this appendix.

|  Component |  Repository location |
|----|----|
|  Tasks, states, edges, chains |  catalog in reproduction/paths.json |
|  Schema, graph, compilation |  src/mcbench/schema.py, graph.py, chains.py |
|  Environment and profiles |  src/mcbench/adapters/minerl.py, profiles.py |
|  Predicates and stage loop |  src/mcbench/verification.py, runner.py |
|  Execution and transfer metrics |  src/mcbench/metrics.py, evolution.py |
|  Paired transfer plan and profiles |  paired_plan, paired_profiles in reproduction/paths.json |
|  Reference memory implementation |  src/mcbench/adapters/jarvis1_online.py |
|  Configuration execution |  src/mcbench/cli.py |

Catalog validation checks the task definitions and compiled chains. A
dry run then exercises the reporting path with the repository’s
diagnostic adapter. Real execution additionally requires the selected
runtime, policy checkpoints, and method-specific dependencies. The
experiment configuration records these choices alongside the catalog
snapshot.
Card [G.6](#A7.SS6 "G.6 Reproduction entry points ‣ Appendix G Prompts and Reproducibility ‣ MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents")
runs from the appendix bundle directory and resolves the catalog through
the companion path map.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A reproducible experiment release associates the frozen catalog,
configuration, model identity, seeds, and artifact identity with each
chain report. Stage evidence and source-cost records preserve the path
from a task definition to a paired contrast.
````
